tagline: Oil, desert and a famous seafront
overview:
Kuwait is a small country at the head of the Persian Gulf, tucked between Iraq and Saudi Arabia and roughly the size of New Jersey. Almost all of it is flat, gravelly desert, and it has no rivers or lakes at all; nearly every drop of drinking water comes from plants that take the salt out of seawater. Kuwait City, the capital, runs along a curving bay, marked by the three Kuwait Towers with their blue-tiled spheres.

About 4.3 million people live in Kuwait, but only around a third are Kuwaiti citizens; the rest are workers and their families from Egypt, India, Bangladesh, the Philippines and elsewhere. Arabic is the official language and English is widely used. Kuwait is a constitutional emirate, led by an emir alongside an elected national assembly that holds more power than most parliaments in the region. Enormous oil reserves make the country wealthy, and its summer heat is among the fiercest on Earth.
landAndNature: Kuwait is desert from end to end, with low ridges, shallow depressions and a coastline of mudflats and shallow bays along the Gulf. Summers are brutal: temperatures above 50 degrees Celsius have been recorded here, among the highest reliably measured anywhere, and shamal winds drive sand across the country. Rain falls only in winter, and after a wet season the desert can bloom briefly with wildflowers. Failaka Island lies offshore, and Bubiyan is a large, almost empty island of salt marsh. Flamingos, herons and crabs feed on the mudflats, while the Gulf holds dugongs, sea turtles and the pearl oysters that divers once hunted.
peopleAndCulture: Kuwaiti life mixes long-standing Gulf traditions with modern city living. The diwaniya, an evening gathering in a room set aside for guests, is where people meet to drink tea, talk politics and trade news, and it remains an important part of public life. Machboos, spiced rice with lamb or fish, is the national dish, and grilled fish from the Gulf is prized. Kuwaiti theater and television dramas are watched across the Arab world. Sea traditions survive in wooden dhow boats and pearl-diving songs. Soccer is followed closely, and in summer the air-conditioned malls serve as the country's town squares.
history: A small fishing and pearling settlement grew on this bay in the early 1700s, and the Al Sabah family has led it since 1752. Kuwaiti dhows traded along the Gulf and across to India, and pearl diving was the main livelihood until cheap cultured pearls from Japan ended the trade in the 1930s. Kuwait became a British protectorate in 1899 and gained full independence on June 19, 1961. Oil, first exported in 1946, transformed it within a single generation from a town of mud houses into a wealthy state. In August 1990 Iraq invaded and occupied Kuwait; an international coalition drove the occupying forces out in February 1991, leaving hundreds of oil wells burning for months.
funFacts: Kuwait has no rivers or lakes, so most of its drinking water is made by removing salt from seawater.
Before oil, Kuwait's wealth came from pearl diving, with divers descending on a single held breath.
Temperatures in Kuwait have passed 50 degrees Celsius, among the hottest ever reliably recorded on the planet.
The Kuwait Towers, opened in 1979, hold water tanks inside the blue-tiled spheres above the seafront.
After oil wells were set alight in 1991, firefighting teams needed about eight months to put out the last of them.
